sentiment.instructions: Judge the feeling the tweet's author actually conveys (about events, people, plans, products), not the topic. Use positive or negative when there is a clear emotional or evaluative cue from the author; otherwise neutral.

criteria.positive: Author shows clear excitement, enjoyment, praise, love, hope or gratitude: 'can't wait', 'excited', 'hyped', 'love', 'best', 'amazing', 'congrats', 'good luck', 'I hope', 'Go team!!', ':)' with an upbeat message. Hype-filled promotions urging people to come, win or support. Approving reports of wins and titles. Sympathy, prayers and RIP wishes. Upbeat teasing.
criteria.neutral: Facts, headlines, scores, schedules, ads, spam, and event or sign-up notices stated informationally. Casual plans or suggestions without emotion words ('going to the game Friday', 'X is the move tomorrow'). Questions, requests to celebrities, trivia and speculation. Wry jokes or ironic commentary on athletes or celebrities without real hostility. Hyperbolic slang and light self-mockery ('I'm dead', 'lmao', a busy day, a paper due). Headlines reporting someone else's criticism. Mixed or mild opinions. When the cues are weak, choose neutral.
criteria.negative: Author clearly expresses anger, disappointment, sadness, frustration, contempt or hostility: 'WTF', 'FML', 'sucks', 'hate', 'worst', 'pissed', 'disappointed', 'so sad', ':(' complaints, insults, profanity aimed at someone, bitter sarcasm, political or religious attacks. Reports centered on clearly harmful events such as attacks, bombings, deaths and losses.
